title: Edamame vs. chickpeas: protein, fiber, and calories

seo.title: Edamame vs. chickpeas: protein, fiber, and calories
seo.meta_description: Edamame is higher in protein and lower in carbs; chickpeas usually provide more fiber. Compare both cooked per 100 g and per serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked edamame and chickpeas for protein, fiber, calories, carbohydrate, fat, and protein quality.

excerpt: Cooked edamame is usually higher in protein and lower in carbohydrate than chickpeas: about 12 g protein and 121 calories per 100 g versus roughly 9 g and 164 calories. Chickpeas generally provide more fiber—around 7–8 g versus about 5 g. Both are nutritious legumes, but edamame is more protein-efficient per calorie.
content_html:
Edamame and chickpeas belong to the same broad food family—legumes—but their macronutrient balance is quite different. Edamame is immature soybean: it carries more protein and fat and much less starch. Mature chickpeas contain more carbohydrate and usually more fiber.

Cooked edamame is higher in protein

The table below compares both foods cooked and ready to eat.

Per 100 g cookedEdamameChickpeas
Protein~12 g~8.9 g
Calories~121 kcal~164 kcal
Carbohydrate~9 g~27 g
Fiber~5 g~7.6 g
Fat~5 g~2.6 g

Edamame provides about 3 g more protein and 43 fewer calories per 100 g. The biggest split is carbohydrate: chickpeas contain roughly three times as much because the mature seed stores much more starch.

A normal serving makes the protein gap visible

At 1 cup cooked, roughly 155 g, edamame provides about 18–19 g protein and close to 190 calories. A similar 155 g amount of chickpeas provides about 14 g protein and roughly 250 calories.

Both can make a meaningful contribution to a meal's protein, but edamame reaches a higher protein amount with less total energy.

Chickpeas win on fiber

A 150 g serving of chickpeas can provide roughly 11–12 g fiber versus about 7–8 g from edamame. Both are good sources, but chickpeas have the clearer advantage here.

Their combination of fiber and starch also explains why their carbohydrate number is higher without meaning the food is mostly sugar.

Edamame's extra fat is not automatically a drawback

Edamame provides about 5 g fat per 100 g, roughly twice as much as chickpeas. Most of that fat is unsaturated, reflecting the natural fat profile of soybeans.

That fat is part of why edamame can have far fewer carbs without being dramatically lower in calories than a simple carb comparison might suggest.

Soy has an especially strong amino acid profile

Soy protein contains all nine essential amino acids in favorable proportions. Chickpeas contain them too, but sulfur-containing amino acids such as methionine are present in lower proportions.

That does not mean chickpeas must be combined with rice at the same meal. A varied diet over the day readily complements amino acids from different plant foods.

Both contribute folate, iron, and minerals

Edamame and chickpeas provide folate, iron, magnesium, and potassium. Their iron is non-heme, so absorption can be improved by eating them with vitamin-C-rich foods.

Which should you choose?

If you want more protein with fewer calories and fewer carbs, edamame has the advantage. If you want more fiber and a starchier legume that supplies more carbohydrate energy, chickpeas fit better.

They complement each other well: these are not two interchangeable beans, but two legumes with distinctly different proportions of protein, fiber, fat, and starch.

faq.question: Which has more protein, edamame or chickpeas?
faq.answer: Cooked edamame provides about 12 g protein per 100 g versus roughly 8.9 g in cooked chickpeas.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Chickpeas usually do: about 7.6 g fiber per 100 g cooked versus roughly 5 g in edamame.

faq.question: Is edamame a complete protein?
faq.answer: Yes. As a soy food, edamame contains all nine essential amino acids in a high-quality plant-protein profile.
